title: Week 11: Logging, Monitoring & SIEM Log Analysis with Wazuh
subject: Information Assurance and Security
description: NIST SP 800-92 log management, Windows/Sysmon/Linux/Network/Cloud telemetry, ingestion pipelines, RFC 5424 Syslog PRIVAL & TLS, anti-forensics prevention, EPS storage tiers, and Wazuh SIEM lab.
sourceFile: BCS411L S2W11 Logging and Monitoring.pdf, BCS411L S2W11 Lab SIEM & Log Analysis v3.pdf

questions.question: According to the Week 11 lecture and NIST SP 800-92, what are the three vital security functions served by logging and monitoring frameworks?
options: 1. Detection & Operational Telemetry, 2. Forensic Reconstruction & Non-Repudiation, and 3. Regulatory Compliance & Assurance
1. Malware Packing, 2. Port Scanning, and 3. Social Engineering
1. File Carving, 2. LSB Steganography, and 3. Disk Encryption
1. Cloud Provisioning, 2. Load Balancing, and 3. DNS Caching
questions.answer: 1. Detection & Operational Telemetry, 2. Forensic Reconstruction & Non-Repudiation, and 3. Regulatory Compliance & Assurance
questions.explanation: Visibility precedes detection, containment, and accountability. Logs enable real-time detection, immutable audit trails (who/what/when/where), and compliance with PCI-DSS Req 10, HIPAA, SOX, and ISO/IEC 27001.

questions.question: Which commands represent offensive anti-forensics techniques attackers use to wipe local audit trails on Windows and Linux?
options: `wevtutil cl` on Windows and `rm -rf /var/log/*` (or `echo "" > /var/log/nginx/access.log`) on Linux
`Get-FileHash` on Windows and `sha256sum` on Linux
`nmap -sS` on Kali and `systemctl status nessusd` on Ubuntu
`strings -a` on Windows and `auditctl -l` on Linux
questions.answer: `wevtutil cl` on Windows and `rm -rf /var/log/*` (or `echo "" > /var/log/nginx/access.log`) on Linux
questions.explanation: Attackers with root/SYSTEM privileges clear Windows Event Logs using `wevtutil cl` or truncate/delete `/var/log/` files on Linux, requiring tamper-resistant remote logging.

questions.question: Which set of Windows Security Log Event IDs correctly matches Successful Logon, Failed Logon, Special Privileges Assigned, and User Account Created?
options: 4624 (Successful Logon), 4625 (Failed Logon), 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned), 4720 (User Account Created)
1 (Successful Logon), 3 (Failed Logon), 6 (Special Privileges), 9 (User Created)
5710 (Successful Logon), 5716 (Failed Logon), 8834 (Special Privileges), 6514 (User Created)
404 (Successful Logon), 500 (Failed Logon), 200 (Special Privileges), 403 (User Created)
questions.answer: 4624 (Successful Logon), 4625 (Failed Logon), 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned), 4720 (User Account Created)
questions.explanation: In the Windows Event Subsystem Security Log: 4624 = Successful Logon, 4625 = Failed Logon, 4672 = Special Privileges Assigned, and 4720 = User Account Created.

questions.question: Why is relying solely on native Windows Event Logs insufficient for detecting Living-off-the-Land (LotL) PowerShell attacks, and how does Sysmon close this gap?
options: Native logs lack granular process execution details; Sysmon tracks process creations with full command-line arguments (Event ID 1), network connections (ID 3), driver loads (ID 6), and raw disk access (ID 9)
Native Windows Event Logs do not record user logins (4624/4625); Sysmon replaces Active Directory
Sysmon automatically blocks all outbound HTTP traffic on port 80 and 443
Sysmon converts Windows EVTX files into Linux `/var/log/syslog` files
questions.answer: Native logs lack granular process execution details; Sysmon tracks process creations with full command-line arguments (Event ID 1), network connections (ID 3), driver loads (ID 6), and raw disk access (ID 9)
questions.explanation: Sysmon extends Windows telemetry by logging process lineage, command-line arguments (Event ID 1), socket connections (Event ID 3), driver loads (Event ID 6), and raw disk access (Event ID 9).

questions.question: On Debian/Ubuntu vs. RHEL/CentOS systems, where are authentication attempts logged, and what does the Linux Audit Subsystem (`auditd`) capture?
options: `/var/log/auth.log` (Debian/Ubuntu) and `/var/log/secure` (RHEL/CentOS); `auditd` captures kernel-level syscalls (`execve`), `/etc/shadow` access, and `sudo` escalations
`C:\Windows\Prefetch` (Debian) and `USRCLASS.DAT` (RHEL); `auditd` captures browser cookies
`/etc/passwd` (Debian) and `/var/ossec` (RHEL); `auditd` captures DNS queries only
`/var/log/nginx` (Debian) and `/tmp/syslog` (RHEL); `auditd` captures NetFlow byte counts only
questions.answer: `/var/log/auth.log` (Debian/Ubuntu) and `/var/log/secure` (RHEL/CentOS); `auditd` captures kernel-level syscalls (`execve`), `/etc/shadow` access, and `sudo` escalations
questions.explanation: Debian/Ubuntu record auth events in `/var/log/auth.log`, RHEL/CentOS use `/var/log/secure`, general system messages go to `/var/log/syslog`, and `auditd` hooks kernel syscalls and sensitive file modifications.

questions.question: How do Flow Records (NetFlow / IPFIX) differ from NIDS/NIPS alerts (Suricata/Snort) in network telemetry?
options: NetFlow/IPFIX summarize conversation metadata (Src/Dst IP, ports, bytes transferred, session duration) without storing packet payloads, whereas Suricata/Snort inspect traffic against signatures/anomalies to emit JSON alerts
NetFlow stores full unencrypted HTTP payloads, whereas Suricata only counts bytes
NetFlow runs inside the Linux kernel via `auditd`, whereas Snort runs only in AWS CloudTrail
Both protocols only log Windows Event ID 4625
questions.answer: NetFlow/IPFIX summarize conversation metadata (Src/Dst IP, ports, bytes transferred, session duration) without storing packet payloads, whereas Suricata/Snort inspect traffic against signatures/anomalies to emit JSON alerts
questions.explanation: NetFlow/IPFIX provide lightweight meta-telemetry (ideal for spotting data exfiltration volumes and C2 beaconing) without payload storage, while NIDS/NIPS generate alerts on malicious traffic patterns.

questions.question: Which telemetry sources detect SQL Injection/XSS web payloads, schema changes (`ALTER`/`DROP`), and cloud management API calls respectively?
options: Web Server Access Logs (Combined Log Format), Database Audit Logs, and Cloud Infrastructure Logs (AWS CloudTrail / Azure Activity Log / GCP Audit Logs)
Sysmon Event ID 6, NetFlow, and Windows Prefetch files
Router ARP tables, LNK files, and EXIF headers
ICMP Echo Replies, Shellbags, and IMDSv1
questions.answer: Web Server Access Logs (Combined Log Format), Database Audit Logs, and Cloud Infrastructure Logs (AWS CloudTrail / Azure Activity Log / GCP Audit Logs)
questions.explanation: Web access logs (Apache/Nginx) record HTTP methods, URIs, and User-Agents; DB audit logs track queries and schema alterations; CloudTrail/Activity/Audit logs capture cloud control-plane API calls.

questions.question: In the Centralized Log Ingestion Pipeline, what is the exact role of the Message Buffer (e.g., Apache Kafka or RabbitMQ)?
options: It sits between Log Shippers (Filebeat/Fluentd) and Ingestion Engines (Logstash/Vector) to queue bursts and prevent log data loss during traffic spikes
It encrypts local Windows Prefetch files before reboot
It serves as the primary Cold Tier archival storage for 7 years
It generates SSH brute-force attacks against Linux endpoints
questions.answer: It sits between Log Shippers (Filebeat/Fluentd) and Ingestion Engines (Logstash/Vector) to queue bursts and prevent log data loss during traffic spikes
questions.explanation: Pipeline flow: Log Sources -> Log Shippers (Filebeat, Fluentd, Syslog-ng, Winlogbeat) -> Message Buffer (Kafka/RabbitMQ) -> Ingestion Engine (Logstash/Vector) -> Storage/SIEM (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Splunk).

questions.question: Using the RFC 3164 / RFC 5424 Syslog formula `PRIVAL = (Facility × 8) + Severity`, what is the Priority Value for a Security/Authorization message (Facility 4) with Critical severity (Severity 2)?
questions.explanation: PRIVAL = (4 × 8) + 2 = 32 + 2 = 34. Facility 4 represents security/authorization messages, and Severity 2 represents Critical conditions.

questions.question: In the Syslog Severity Levels (0–7), which level represents the MOST urgent condition ('System is unusable') and which represents the LEAST urgent ('Debug-level messages')?
options: 0 = Emergency (`emerg`, most urgent) and 7 = Debug (`debug`, least urgent)
7 = Emergency (`emerg`, most urgent) and 0 = Debug (`debug`, least urgent)
1 = Critical (`crit`, most urgent) and 10 = Info (`info`, least urgent)
0 = Informational (`info`, most urgent) and 7 = Alert (`alert`, least urgent)
questions.answer: 0 = Emergency (`emerg`, most urgent) and 7 = Debug (`debug`, least urgent)
questions.explanation: Syslog severity descends in urgency from 0 (Emergency), 1 (Alert), 2 (Critical), 3 (Error), 4 (Warning), 5 (Notice), 6 (Informational), to 7 (Debug).

questions.question: Why is legacy Syslog on UDP Port 514 insecure, and what modern standard secures Syslog in transit?
options: UDP 514 is unencrypted and vulnerable to sniffing/spoofing; secure deployments enforce Syslog over TLS on TCP Port 6514
UDP 514 compresses logs too aggressively; modern Syslog uses ICMP Echo
UDP 514 only works on Windows; modern Syslog uses SMB Port 445
UDP 514 requires client-side HYOK keys; modern Syslog uses Telnet Port 23
questions.answer: UDP 514 is unencrypted and vulnerable to sniffing/spoofing; secure deployments enforce Syslog over TLS on TCP Port 6514
questions.explanation: Syslog over TLS (TCP Port 6514) provides confidentiality, server authentication, and transport integrity unlike cleartext UDP 514.

questions.question: An attacker compromises a web server and immediately runs `echo "" > /var/log/nginx/access.log`. Which architectural control prevents this from wiping evidence from the central SOC?
options: Real-time log forwarding (Write-Only Remote Logging) streaming events immediately off-host to a hardened central collector, paired with WORM storage and RBAC
Leaving logs solely on `/var/log/nginx/` with 777 permissions
Switching the web server from Apache to Nginx
Running a weekly cron job to copy logs to `/tmp`
questions.answer: Real-time log forwarding (Write-Only Remote Logging) streaming events immediately off-host to a hardened central collector, paired with WORM storage and RBAC
questions.explanation: Streaming logs in real time to an out-of-band collector ensures historical events already exist centrally before the attacker clears local disk logs.

questions.question: How do Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) storage and rolling HMAC-SHA256 cryptographic hash chains protect centralized logs?
options: WORM prevents physical/logical modification or deletion of written blocks, and HMAC-SHA256 hash chains cause validation checks to fail if any sequential entry is inserted, edited, or deleted
WORM automatically deletes logs every 30 days, while HMAC-SHA256 compresses JSON into ZIP files
WORM gives SOC analysts write/delete permissions on all index volumes
HMAC-SHA256 allows attackers to modify historical timestamps silently
questions.answer: WORM prevents physical/logical modification or deletion of written blocks, and HMAC-SHA256 hash chains cause validation checks to fail if any sequential entry is inserted, edited, or deleted
questions.explanation: WORM storage, rolling cryptographic hash chains, and strict RBAC (read-only for analysts, write-only for ingestion pipelines) safeguard log integrity.

questions.question: Using `DailyStorage (Bytes) = AverageEPS × AverageEventSize (Bytes) × 86,400`, how much uncompressed daily log storage is required for 5,000 EPS at an average event size of 800 bytes?
options: 31.1 TB/day
4.0 MB/day
86.4 GB/day
questions.explanation: 5,000 × 800 × 86,400 = 345,600,000,000 Bytes ≈ 345.6 GB/day (which equals ~31.1 TB over a 90-day retention period).

questions.question: Which Log Storage Lifecycle Tier uses high-speed NVMe/SSD for real-time SIEM correlation with sub-second search performance (typically 0 to 30 days)?
options: Hot Tier
Warm Tier
Cold Tier
Frozen / Archive Tier
questions.answer: Hot Tier
questions.explanation: Hot Tier (NVMe/SSD, 0–30 days) supports sub-second real-time correlation; Warm (HDD/Cloud Volumes, 31–90 days) takes seconds–minutes; Cold (S3, 91–365 days) requires re-indexing; Frozen (Glacier, 1–7+ years) takes hours to restore.

questions.question: Which storage tier is specifically designed for long-term legal compliance and regulatory retention (1 to 7+ years) using solutions like AWS Glacier where restoration takes hours?
options: Frozen / Archive Tier
Hot Tier
Warm Tier
Message Buffer Tier
questions.answer: Frozen / Archive Tier
questions.explanation: The Frozen / Archive Tier (e.g., Glacier) provides compressed, unindexed long-term archival retention (1–7+ years) at lowest cost, with multi-hour restore times.

questions.question: How should an organization balance security visibility against storage costs, ingestion bottlenecks, and alert fatigue when designing log pipelines?
options: Filter noisy/benign debug telemetry at the shipper, buffer spikes with Kafka/RabbitMQ, route logs through Hot/Warm/Cold/Frozen storage tiers, and tune correlation/RBA rules
Log every single debug packet into Hot NVMe SSDs for 7 years without filtering
Disable logging on all endpoints and only log printer errors
Eliminate message buffers and forward UDP 514 straight to Glacier
questions.answer: Filter noisy/benign debug telemetry at the shipper, buffer spikes with Kafka/RabbitMQ, route logs through Hot/Warm/Cold/Frozen storage tiers, and tune correlation/RBA rules
questions.explanation: Strategic filtering, message buffering, tiered storage retention, and tuned alerting maintain high-value visibility without breaking budgets or overwhelming analysts.

questions.question: In the Week 11 Wazuh lab, what three central components are installed on VM 1 (Wazuh Server) by `sudo bash ./wazuh-install.sh -a`?
options: Wazuh Manager, Wazuh Indexer, and Wazuh Dashboard
Nmap, Nessus, and Autopsy
Filebeat, RabbitMQ, and Wireshark
Ghidra, x64dbg, and Volatility
questions.answer: Wazuh Manager, Wazuh Indexer, and Wazuh Dashboard
questions.explanation: The automated Wazuh quickstart assistant (`-a`) deploys the central Wazuh Manager, Indexer, and Dashboard onto VM 1 (`192.168.56.10`).

questions.question: In Part 2 of the Wazuh lab, how is the Wazuh Agent on VM 2 configured to point to the central Wazuh Manager during APT installation?
options: By passing the manager IP as an environment variable: `sudo WAZUH_MANAGER="192.168.56.10" apt-get install wazuh-agent -y`
By editing `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts` on VM 1
By running `sudo nmap -sS 192.168.56.10` from VM 2
By uploading `/var/log/auth.log` manually to VirusTotal
questions.answer: By passing the manager IP as an environment variable: `sudo WAZUH_MANAGER="192.168.56.10" apt-get install wazuh-agent -y`
questions.explanation: After importing the Wazuh GPG key and adding the repo, `WAZUH_MANAGER="192.168.56.10"` registers the agent with VM 1 during installation, followed by enabling/starting `wazuh-agent`.

questions.question: Where is the default Wazuh agent configuration file located on a Linux endpoint, and which XML element defines which local log files are monitored?
options: `/var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf`, using the `<localfile>` element
`/etc/nmap/nmap.conf`, using the `<script>` element
`/var/log/wazuh.json`, using the `<syslog>` element
`/opt/nessus/nessus.ini`, using the `<plugin>` element
questions.answer: `/var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf`, using the `<localfile>` element
questions.explanation: On Linux endpoints, `/var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf` configures the Wazuh agent, and `<localfile>` blocks specify log paths (such as `/var/log/auth.log`) and log formats to monitor.

questions.question: In Step 3.2 of the Wazuh lab, which command simulates unauthorized SSH login attempts and which local file records those raw failure events?
options: `ssh non_existent_user@localhost` with 3–5 failed password attempts, logged to `/var/log/auth.log`
`curl https://192.168.56.10:8834`, logged to `/var/log/nginx/error.log`
`sudo dpkg -i wazuh.deb`, logged to `/etc/shadow`
`strings -a sshd`, logged to `~/.bash_history`
questions.answer: `ssh non_existent_user@localhost` with 3–5 failed password attempts, logged to `/var/log/auth.log`
questions.explanation: Attempting SSH logins as `non_existent_user@localhost` generates failed authentication entries inside `/var/log/auth.log`, which the Wazuh agent forwards to the Manager.

questions.question: When filtering Security Events in the Wazuh Dashboard with `rule.groups: "sshd"`, what do Rule ID 5710 and Rule ID 5716 represent?
options: Rule ID 5710 = `sshd: Attempt to login using non-existent user`; Rule ID 5716 = `sshd: Authentication failed`
Rule ID 5710 = `Windows User Account Created`; Rule ID 5716 = `Sysmon Raw Disk Access`
Rule ID 5710 = `Nmap SYN Scan Detected`; Rule ID 5716 = `S3 Public Access Blocked`
Rule ID 5710 = `Kernel Panic`; Rule ID 5716 = `Wazuh Agent Disconnected`
questions.answer: Rule ID 5710 = `sshd: Attempt to login using non-existent user`; Rule ID 5716 = `sshd: Authentication failed`
questions.explanation: The lab triggers both Wazuh rules: Rule ID 5710 (Level 5) for attempting login with a non-existent user and Rule ID 5716 for failed SSH authentication.

questions.question: When expanding an SSH alert in the Wazuh Dashboard, which normalized fields show the source IP address, severity classification, and raw log line?
options: `data.srcip`, `rule.level`, and `full_log`
`cvss.base`, `plugin.output`, and `nmap.os`
`mft.flag`, `exif.gps`, and `entropy.score`
`syslog.prival`, `worm.hash`, and `imds.token`
questions.answer: `data.srcip`, `rule.level`, and `full_log`
questions.explanation: Step 3.3 highlights `agent.name` (endpoint name), `data.srcip` (`127.0.0.1`), `rule.level` (severity), and `full_log` (raw log line ingested from `/var/log/auth.log`).

questions.question: How does the Wazuh Manager transform raw text logs from endpoints into categorized security alerts inside the SIEM dashboard?
options: Decoders first parse and extract structured fields (program name, source IP, username) from raw log strings; Rules then evaluate those decoded fields against conditions and thresholds to assign Rule IDs, levels, and rule groups
The Wazuh Dashboard runs `strings -a` on the Linux kernel directly
Wazuh Manager uses hardware write-blockers to carve JPEG headers out of `/var/log/auth.log`
Decoders delete raw logs while Rules forward alerts over unencrypted UDP 514
questions.answer: Decoders first parse and extract structured fields (program name, source IP, username) from raw log strings; Rules then evaluate those decoded fields against conditions and thresholds to assign Rule IDs, levels, and rule groups
questions.explanation: Wazuh's analysis engine uses a two-stage pipeline: Decoders normalize raw text into key-value attributes, and Rules match patterns/frequencies to generate categorized alerts.

questions.question: In RFC 3164 / RFC 5424 Syslog, which Facility Code range is reserved for local custom use (`local0` through `local7`), and what does Facility 0 represent?
options: 16–23 for `local0`–`local7`; Facility 0 represents kernel messages
0–7 for `local0`–`local7`; Facility 0 represents user-level debug
10–15 for `local0`–`local7`; Facility 0 represents AWS CloudTrail
24–31 for `local0`–`local7`; Facility 0 represents SSH authentication
questions.answer: 16–23 for `local0`–`local7`; Facility 0 represents kernel messages
questions.explanation: Syslog Facility Codes span 0–23: 0 = kernel messages, 3 = system daemons, 4 = security/authorization messages, and 16–23 = local0–local7.

questions.question: What fields are recorded in a standard Apache/Nginx Combined Log Format entry, and what attacks do they help detect?
options: Client IP, Timestamp, HTTP Method, URI Query, Status Code, and User-Agent; detects SQL Injection, Path Traversal, and XSS
CPU Register, RAM Offset, and DLL Import Table; detects UPX packing
GPS Latitude, Camera Model, and UTC Offset; detects Steganography
IAM Role ARN, S3 Bucket ACL, and KMS Key ID; detects SSRF
questions.answer: Client IP, Timestamp, HTTP Method, URI Query, Status Code, and User-Agent; detects SQL Injection, Path Traversal, and XSS
questions.explanation: Combined Log Format captures HTTP request context including URI query strings and User-Agent headers, making it essential for spotting SQLi, Path Traversal, and XSS probes.

questions.question: What security events are captured by Identity Providers (IdPs) such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, and Active Directory?
options: Single Sign-On (SSO) requests, Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) prompts, and conditional access rule enforcement
Hard disk sector slack space and NTFS $Bitmap flips
Kernel `execve` system calls and `/etc/shadow` reads
TCP Window Size and IP Identifier sequence generation
questions.answer: Single Sign-On (SSO) requests, Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) prompts, and conditional access rule enforcement
questions.explanation: IdP logs monitor identity-plane authentication, MFA fatigue/prompts, SSO token issuance, and conditional access evaluations.

questions.question: In the Centralized Log Ingestion Pipeline diagram, which tools act as lightweight Log Shippers vs. Ingestion Engines that parse, normalize, and enrich logs?
options: Log Shippers: Filebeat, Fluentd, Syslog-ng, Winlogbeat; Ingestion Engines: Logstash and Vector
Log Shippers: Elasticsearch and Splunk; Ingestion Engines: Apache and Nginx
Log Shippers: Volatility and FTK Imager; Ingestion Engines: Ghidra and IDA Pro
Log Shippers: AWS Glacier and S3; Ingestion Engines: Suricata and Snort
questions.answer: Log Shippers: Filebeat, Fluentd, Syslog-ng, Winlogbeat; Ingestion Engines: Logstash and Vector
questions.explanation: Endpoint/server shippers (Filebeat, Fluentd, Syslog-ng, Winlogbeat) forward logs through Kafka/RabbitMQ into Logstash or Vector for parsing/enrichment before indexing in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Splunk.

questions.question: How should Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) be enforced on a centralized SIEM or logging engine under Least Privilege?
options: Security analysts receive read-only query access, while write/delete permissions on index volumes are restricted strictly to automated ingestion pipelines
All SOC analysts share the `admin` account with full index deletion rights
Linux endpoints are given root SSH access to the SIEM indexers
Write permissions are granted publicly so external threat feeds can edit historical logs
questions.answer: Security analysts receive read-only query access, while write/delete permissions on index volumes are restricted strictly to automated ingestion pipelines
questions.explanation: Restricting analysts to read-only queries ensures neither compromised analyst credentials nor insiders can alter or purge historical audit indices.

questions.question: What differentiates the Warm Tier from the Cold Tier in a tiered log lifecycle architecture?
options: Warm Tier (31–90 days) uses HDD/Cloud Volumes with active indices queried in seconds–minutes; Cold Tier (91–365 days) uses compressed read-only Object Storage (S3) requiring re-indexing
Warm Tier uses NVMe SSDs for 7 years; Cold Tier uses CPU cache for 5 minutes
Warm Tier stores unencrypted UDP logs; Cold Tier stores live Windows Registry hives
Warm Tier has slower searches than the Frozen Glacier tier
questions.answer: Warm Tier (31–90 days) uses HDD/Cloud Volumes with active indices queried in seconds–minutes; Cold Tier (91–365 days) uses compressed read-only Object Storage (S3) requiring re-indexing
questions.explanation: Warm storage keeps 31–90 day logs actively indexed on slower HDD/cloud volumes for investigations, whereas Cold storage compresses 91–365 day logs into S3/Blob object storage requiring re-indexing before querying.

questions.question: After starting `wazuh-agent` on VM 2 in the lab, how do you verify on VM 1's Wazuh Dashboard that the endpoint registered properly?
options: Navigate to Endpoints / Agents in the Wazuh Dashboard and confirm VM 2 appears with a status of `Active`
Run `sudo nmap -O 192.168.56.20` from VM 1
Check `Results -> EXIF Metadata` in Autopsy
Inspect the S3 Block Public Access tab in AWS Console
questions.answer: Navigate to Endpoints / Agents in the Wazuh Dashboard and confirm VM 2 appears with a status of `Active`
questions.explanation: Step 3.1 verifies registration by checking that the Linux endpoint appears as `Active` under Endpoints / Agents in the Wazuh Dashboard.

questions.question: Which Sysmon Event ID is specifically valuable for detecting suspicious kernel-mode rootkit or driver loading, and which tracks raw disk access?
options: Event ID 6 (Driver Loading) and Event ID 9 (Raw Disk Access)
Event ID 1 (Driver Loading) and Event ID 3 (Raw Disk Access)
Event ID 4624 (Driver Loading) and Event ID 4720 (Raw Disk Access)
Event ID 5710 (Driver Loading) and Event ID 5716 (Raw Disk Access)
questions.answer: Event ID 6 (Driver Loading) and Event ID 9 (Raw Disk Access)
questions.explanation: The Week 11 lecture highlights Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Creation), ID 3 (Network Connections), ID 6 (Driver Loading), and ID 9 (Raw Disk Access).
